expectations.description: Each of the four references medians >= 4 over 3 runs (the mean is reported, not gated)
LEGO story with Juno's name removed from all but one chapter scores center <= 2
expectations.detail: center=2 (raw), kept in "Chapter 1: The Carpenter in Billund", 12 mentions removed. Evidence: Milo is active throughout: he spots the 1932 calendar, finds that the first brick falls off, suggests the tubes and shakes the clicked bricks. Juno, the worst-covered child, acts by name only in Chapter 1 ('Uh oh', pulling the duck). After that, lines that should be hers go to Milo ('Milo grabbed Milo's hand', 'Milo carried planks. Milo handed out nails.', the closing two-voice exchange), so she shares only group shouts like 'LEGO!' across roughly four of ten chapters and is silent for three or more consecutive chapters.

expectations.description: Soccer story with three invented dates scores facts <= 2 and the evidence names at least two of them
expectations.detail: facts=2 (raw); named 3/3 injected dates (1847, 1911, 1926). Evidence: Several dates are wrong and appear both in the story and in the True Facts list. The Football Association was formed in 1863, not 1847. The penalty kick was adopted in 1891, not 1911. The first World Cup was in 1930, not 1926. McCrum's Milford was in Ireland before partition, so "Northern Ireland" is anachronistic. The 'thought it was a typo' legend is stated without a hedge. Much else is accurate: cuju, Pickles, Pelé, the cards, Dick, Kerr Ladies, Chastain and Messi.

expectations.description: Shark story where the great white chases and rams the submarine scores age_fit <= 2 for band A
expectations.detail: age_fit=2 (raw); word count 1851 -> 1826, length effectively unchanged so this is peril and not padding. 'Milo smashed his shoulder into the wall'. The chapter ends with the boys silent in black water. The rest of the story fits a 4-year-old well, with short lines, SPLOOSH and shout-alongs, and the 1826 words fall within the ±15% tolerance.

scenarios.why: F13: band A pair, second story on sharks. Tests series continuity against a real bible.
scenarios.best_moment: Juno's eyes went huge. "Five hundred?! I only know ten numbers!"
scenarios.worst_moment: "I see you, Juno! And I see... wait, there's no ceiling here."
editor_notes: Fix the first True Facts entry so it matches the story and the science: sharks lived more than 400 million years ago, long before dinosaurs (about 200 million years earlier).
Pay off the LEGO shark that swims out and grows: make it become Finn, or have it swim alongside and shrink back at the end, so the opening image isn't dropped.

scenarios.why: F13: band C second story on history-of-soccer. Continuity with a guide character.

notes: narrative word count 1791 is outside 2200-3200 ±15%

scenarios.best_moment: Across the field, a crowd of players in loose tunics kicked a stitched leather ball back and forth with only their feet, chasing it like it owed them money.
scenarios.worst_moment: "That's the exact rule I just wrote in the last chapter."
editor_notes: Give Theo a hands-on beat in each of Chapters 5–8. He could take a shot in the 1872 match, help an official decide what a yellow card means, or test his league idea on McGregor. This would turn Bit's lectures into scenes and naturally bring the story up into the word range.
Make each coin a 'saved level' as the bible requires: something goes wrong at each stop and Theo's builder thinking fixes it. Split the crowded Chapter 7 into two stops.

Fix the factual slips: McGregor was a draper, Aston devised the cards rather than refereeing in 1970, and Morley's first Laws were not simply 'feet only'. Also fix the callback 'the exact rule I just wrote', since Theo's rules were about the field and the number of players, not hands.

scenarios.why: F13: mixed ages 4, 7 and 10 on volcanoes. Band follows the youngest; the 10-year-old still needs a hook per chapter.

notes: gate reported 2 hard violation(s)

scenarios.best_moment: Juno yawned a giant yawn. "Still not a dinosaur." Theo grinned. "Nope. Better."
scenarios.worst_moment: Same hot insides, just different outsides.
editor_notes: Fix the Hawaii science and merge Chapters 3 and 4 into one Hawaii stop: runny lava spreads out flat like pancake batter, and sticky lava piles up tall like Fuji. Let Theo's 'Why is it round and not pointy?' get that real answer, and use the freed chapter for a fresh discovery.

Give each child a hands-on beat at the volcanoes, which will also lift the word count into range. For example, Juno could stomp her dinosaur to make the seismograph wiggle, Milo could stack bricks to measure three Everests against Olympus Mons, and Theo could choose the route on Sizzle's map. Juno also needs a real moment in Iceland beyond looking for dinosaurs.

Soften the material for the 4-year-old and tidy the loose ends. Drop 'cover whole states in ash' and the 'years and years before' overclaim, and cut 'Nobody cared' about bedtime. Change 'yummy dirt' to something like 'super-strong soil' and remove Sizzle's sleeve. Add a shout-along line to every chapter, not just four.

scenarios.why: F13: 5-minute band A on bees. The shortest target - tests that word targets scale.
scenarios.best_moment: "RAINDROP!" Juno shouted, waving her arms. The other bees scooted inside, just in time.
scenarios.worst_moment: I got stuck inside it, long, long ago. Even before your dinosaurs!
editor_notes: Fix the dinosaur timeline in Chapter 1. Change "Even before your dinosaurs!" to something like "Back when your dinosaurs were stomping around!" so it matches Chapter 7 and the True Facts list.

Rework Chapter 7 around a Juno action instead of a fact recital. Cut or soften the "way before pyramids" beekeeping claim, and hedge the Egyptian honey ("People say pots of honey found in old Egyptian tombs were still good to eat").

Untangle Chapters 5-6. Let Juno land on a flower and sip nectar herself first, then fly home and do the waggle dance, so the honey-making journey runs in order and she does something hands-on in Chapter 6.

scenarios.why: F13: 15-minute band C on space-race. The longest target - tests that length does not become padding.
scenarios.best_moment: He added one more line afterward, almost without thinking about it: a message that only appeared if a player's tether broke, two words glowing steady against the dark — HOLD ON.
scenarios.worst_moment: Theo let out a breath he hadn't noticed he'd been holding.
editor_notes: Fix Level 2's broken logic. Cut the orphaned 'No,' agreed Control reply and the soccer-ball-inspired-the-mascot line, or make them follow from what came before. Reveal the team name Theo types, since the story sets it up as funny.

Correct the small factual slips. Use 'about 12 minutes' for Leonov. Compare the 108-minute flight to 'shorter than a soccer match with extra time'. Replace the marathon comparison with something that conveys orbital distance, and don't have Control endorse it.

Tighten the prose for read-aloud. Remove the 'breath he hadn't noticed he'd been holding' cliché, vary the repeated stage business, and trim stacked intensifiers. Also change 'since the very first night of this project' so the one-night timeline holds.

scenarios.why: F13: a sensitive-but-allowed topic, band B. Must pass with scary_level <= 1.
scenarios.best_moment: Maya's crayon hovered over her sketchbook. "That's not fair math."
scenarios.worst_moment: "Everyone's safe now," Maya said, drawing the rescue ship with its lights glowing bright against the dark water.
editor_notes: Fix the factual slips in both the story and the True Facts list. Harland and Wolff workers built Titanic for the White Star Line. The fourth funnel mainly carried ventilation, not just looks. Replace 'Nobody panics... just like a fire drill' with something gentle but honest, such as many people didn't believe the ship could sink, so some lifeboats left half-full.

Add one calm, simple sentence that the ship slowly sank. Use it to answer Maya's 'two rooms' question: the iceberg opened about five or six compartments, too many to stay afloat. Change 'Everyone's safe now' to 'Everyone in the lifeboats is safe now', so the cheer doesn't contradict the 1,500 lost.

Use the roughly 200 words needed to reach the target range to bring in Maya's love of swimming. For example, her swim towel could prompt Pip to explain why lifejackets and lifeboats matter in cold sea water. Cut the moralizing 'biggest lessons this story teaches us' line in favour of Maya's own words.

scenarios.why: #48: A5 cell. A three-year-old, the youngest band edge, on a gentle science topic.

notes: narrative word count 515 is outside 650-850 ±15%

scenarios.best_moment: "Goodnight, Ivy," he whispered. "Paint bright, dream bright."
scenarios.worst_moment: Ivy smiled a big smile. "A rainbow pops up right after it rains. When the sun peeks out!"
editor_notes: Explain where the colours come from: white sunlight is really all the colours mixed together, and bending spreads them out. Tie it to painting, for example Ivy seeing every colour of her paint box hiding inside one beam of light. This is the heart of 'how rainbows form' and the story currently skips it.

Give puddles a real scene and fix the cloud-to-fountain jump. For instance, land Ivy beside a sunny puddle and a sprinkler or fountain rather than on a cloud, and let her splash to make mist and her own rainbow. This adds the 50-150 words needed to reach the target range and makes the title true.

Let Ivy make one choice or idea of her own (such as deciding to turn around, or suggesting the mist). Also correct the home painting to show the sun low behind her rather than 'up high', and trim the True Facts list to lines that actually appear in the story.

scenarios.why: #48: A5 cell. A note about a bedtime fear - the story must soothe it, never feed it.
scenarios.best_moment: Leo squeezed his eyes shut and wiggled them, giggling. "I can't tell if mine are dancing!" he laughed.
scenarios.worst_moment: He did not feel scared of the dark anymore. His tiny clock was ready. His sleepy juice was working.
editor_notes: Earn the dark-fear resolution instead of stating it. Pay off Station Three ('Dark puts it to sleep') so Leo realises the dark is his tiny clock's helper, and let him choose to dim his own night-light on the last page.

Rework the melatonin stop: don't have Leo pretend to catch and drink 'sleepy juice' from bottles, or compare it to cocoa. Make clear his own brain makes it inside him, so no child asks for a bottle at bedtime. Also fix the 'Only while you sleep' growth line and soften 'owls sleep all day' to 'many owls'.

Lighten the lecture load. Merge back-to-back 'said Hoot' tags and drop Eugene, Lerner and the dates for band A. Cut or combine one station so the tour builds toward a sleepiest final stop and lands inside 850 words.

scenarios.why: #48: A15 cell (was empty), and a third story in the Milo and Juno series. The longest band A target - padding is the risk.
scenarios.best_moment: Every bird outside your window is a dinosaur's great-great-great-grandchild. Dinosaurs never really left. They just got smaller. They grew wings. They learned to sing.
scenarios.worst_moment: A long, long time after all this — about 66 million years later — the world changed a whole lot, all at once.
editor_notes: Fix the factual slips. Change 'about 66 million years later' to 'about 66 million years ago,' cut the invented 'He just liked how it sounded,' and replace the 'bone detective' etymology with 'a scientist who studies ancient life.' Then add one line acknowledging that the brick is hopping between different dinosaur times, since Stegosaurus and T. rex never met.

Give the middle a shape. Thread one small goal through the tour, such as Milo collecting ideas for his LEGO build or Juno finding a name for her nameless green dinosaur, and pay it off at home. Also fix the 'one more stop' signposting.

Soften the T. rex entrance for a 4-year-old with a gentler, sillier hello rather than a roar that sends Juno hiding. Cut the repeated turkey-size exposition in Chapter 5, and add shout-along lines to chapters 3, 7 and 8.

Give Dev a meaningful action in Chapters 2, 5 and 10, for example spraying the prism wall in Newton's room to make a second spectrum. Turn Chapter 9's myth list into a beat: the kids try to chase the rainbow's end and watch it move away.

scenarios.why: #48: B10 cell, a new care topic. A town lost to a volcano, told to a 7-year-old: true, and calm.
scenarios.best_moment: It's like the whole town took a nap and never finished breakfast.
scenarios.worst_moment: A bakery cat stretched in a sunny doorway, very much alive, just a memory brought to light.
editor_notes: Fix the time-travel logic. Either Nora visits living Pompeii in 79 AD (fresh, warm bread, a real cat) or she visits ruins, but not both in one scene. Move the 'ash froze the town' reveal out of the bakery so the eruption in ch6 lands fresh.

Correct the anachronisms. Move the plaster-cast pouring to a later scene (the 1860s, with Giuseppe Fiorelli). Show Pliny the Younger watching from Misenum and writing his letters years later. Hedge the August 24 date ('long thought to be August 24 — some scientists now think autumn').

Use Nora's love of mosaics inside Pompeii itself. Let her find the 'Cave Canem' dog mosaic or the Alexander Mosaic, or spot a missing tessera that Tessa came from. Give her one real choice of where to go next, and trim the repeated 'almost two thousand years' and 'gently.'

scenarios.why: #48: B15 cell (was empty). Maya's series continues with Barnacle, and Apollo 1 is a care fact at age 7.

scenarios.best_moment: "It's like footprints on a beach," she whispered, "except they'll never wash away."
scenarios.worst_moment: "Sputnik gave the United States a scare," Barnacle explained.
editor_notes: Bring the story up to target length by giving Maya more to do. Let her drawings change what happens in more chapters, as the password did in Chapter 1. For example, her sketch could steer the porthole, or she could help 'fix' the Apollo 13 scene step by step. Let her ask 'why' questions that drive the next scene.

Break the 'That's X, on [date]' lecture formula. Let some facts be discovered through Maya's actions or questions, vary the scene entrances, and keep the chronology clean by moving Shepard before the Kennedy speech.

Strengthen continuity and voice. Open with a nod to the bridge story's final rivet, and give Barnacle his promised bad pun in each chapter (for example, 'seal of approval' or 'orbit-rary'). This also adds the parent-level humour the prose currently lacks.

scenarios.why: #48: B15 cell. Where the volcanoes scenario broke rule 10 (a stick in a hot spring) - now for a child who collects rocks.
scenarios.best_moment: "The ocean has muscles," Zara said, impressed.
scenarios.worst_moment: Stack almost three Mount Everests, and you'd still look up at it.
editor_notes: Give the journey a through-line and a touch of mystery, such as a question the geode needs Zara to answer or a crystal she collects at each stop. That would make the 'They landed…' chapters build toward something instead of reading as a list. Split Chapter 8's three locations so the expanded length reaches the 2,400-word target.

Fix the factual slips. Olympus Mons is about two and a half Everests tall, so 'stack almost three and still look up' is wrong. Say magma forms in hot pockets deep underground rather than implying all rock below the crust is melted. Make the True Facts Krakatoa line match the story's wording.

Turn the 'Ember explained' summary paragraphs into hands-on moments for Zara, such as pushing two puzzle-piece plates together or feeling the seismograph needle wiggle. Also resolve the pebble: either it moves from her pocket into the geode, or it is a deliberate second gift.

scenarios.why: #48: B15 cell. A long story on a topic the children know better than the writer - accuracy and no brand worship.

notes: narrative word count 1865 is outside 2400-3300 ±15%

scenarios.best_moment: "Some say he got the idea from a pizza missing one slice." Ben laughed. "That's the best reason to invent anything ever."
scenarios.worst_moment: "Falling blocks,
editor_notes: Add about 300–500 words, ideally by giving Chapters 7 and 8 a real hands-on beat for Ben. For example, he could design a level, test the Wii remote himself, or build something in Minecraft with Pixel instead of watching a list of consoles go by.

Fix the copy errors a parent will trip over aloud: 'finishizing,' the cut-off '"Falling blocks,' line in Chapter 6, and the repeated 'basically.' Also align the Chapter 7 date range with the 1994 PlayStation.
Vary Ben's role so he isn't fixing every grown-up's machine. Let some chapters turn on a question he asks, a choice he makes, or a discovery that surprises him, so the shape doesn't feel formulaic.

scenarios.why: #48: C5 cell (was empty). The shortest band C target - a lot of history in few words.
scenarios.best_moment: "Nobody scores," the ball said. "It ends 0–0. Historians call it the birth of international football. The goalkeepers call it a great shift."
scenarios.worst_moment: Brazil, meanwhile, was busy becoming the most decorated team in history, eventually winning it five times, with a forward named Pele on three of those winning squads — the only player ever to manage that.
editor_notes: Fix the Morley scene. The 1863 Laws allowed a fair catch but had no goalkeeper exception, so either move Lena's 'Except for one person' moment to the 1870–71 change that created the keeper's handling role, or have Morley admit there is no keeper yet and let Lena argue for one. That would be historically true and gives her a real choice.

Give Lena a hands-on beat or decision in the lecture-heavy chapters. For example, have her make a save in the 1872 match, help spot the trophy alongside Pickles, or kick a ball with the Dick, Kerr Ladies in a real 1920 scene. This would also fix Ch7, which is told rather than shown, out of order and with no setting.

Clean up the internal slips and the band mismatch. Make it 'over 2,000 years' in both places, have the tennis ball turn up under the bed in Ch8 as a callback, cut the band-A-style bolded shout-lines, and trim the Brazil/Ken Aston fact dump from Ch6.

scenarios.why: #48: C5 cell. A child who fights bedtime: persuasive without lecturing, and ends sleepy.
scenarios.best_moment: "So his brain's doing backflips, and his body's just... lying there like a sack of kit bags."
scenarios.worst_moment: It hummed — the exact hum of a cricket ball snicked clean for six.
editor_notes: Make the promised "Real case" real. Give Captain REM a problem Arjun solves across the chapters, for example a sleepless hero who can't nod off until Arjun applies each discovery. That way the middle chapters build toward something instead of reading as interchangeable fact stops.

Cut the standalone bold shout-lines after each chapter and the doubled ending. Keep the shouts inside the scenes, where they work, and end on one final line rather than restating "five more minutes" twice. This suits a 9-year-old listener better.

Tighten the details a cricket- and comics-loving kid will catch. Replace "snicked clean for six" with something accurate ("a ball struck clean for six"). Either give "Lights out" to Arjun earlier or rework the "That's my line" joke. Drop the "(1953)" from the Chapter 1 heading, since the chapter opens in the present day.

scenarios.why: #48: C5 cell. An older child on an invention story - mystery tone without inventing facts.
scenarios.best_moment: "The pedals are fighting the steering," he said. "Every time you turn, you're fighting your own legs."
scenarios.worst_moment: Tom stood holding his bike, chain fixed without him even noticing, Spoke cooling in his palm.
editor_notes: Let Tom fix his own chain at the end using something he learned on the journey, such as how Starley's chain seats on the sprocket. This pays off the cold open through his engineering instead of by magic.

Break up the chapter 8 fact rush. Either give the 1970s mountain-bike pioneers a short scene of their own, since they are 'your people, Tom', or trim derailleurs, the Tour and the billion-bike figure to one line. Then end on a sharper, more mysterious final image of Spoke.

Hedge the disputed Michaux/Lallement pedal credit with a light in-story line, for example 'they still argue about who did it first'. Also fix the 'hard rubber wheels' slip and cut the repeated 'already' and 'great-great-grand' phrasings.

scenarios.why: #48: C10 cell. The Titanic for a 10-year-old: more of the truth than band B, still bedtime-safe.
scenarios.best_moment: "That's not how atlases work," she said, which was true, but she climbed toward the page anyway, because a girl who loves maps does not ignore one that is clearly alive.
scenarios.worst_moment: Go tell the wireless room. They need to start calling for help, now, while there's still plenty of time to get everyone off safely.
editor_notes: Fix the factual slips: put Ballard aboard the research ship Knorr watching Argo's camera feed, give Carpathia's distance as about 58 nautical miles, say the forward holds and boiler rooms flooded rather than the engine rooms, and cut the officer's 'plenty of time to get everyone off safely,' which undercuts the lifeboat-gap lesson.
Give Hana an active beat in Chapter 7. She could use her map instinct to plot where the lifeboats are drifting, or work out the 1,178-vs-2,224 gap herself, instead of being told it over tea.

Smooth the time jumps ('come back tomorrow' / 'the day before'), fix the confusing 'glowing letters still curling off her map at home' line, and swap the band-A-style bold shout lines for one dry, older-kid joke per chapter to lean into both the mystery tone and band C humour.

scenarios.why: #48: C10 cell. Competitive brothers: rule 9 - rivalry without put-downs.
